extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners), patent counsel, small entities, and USPTO staff administering IPR/PGR/CBM proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural standards for preparing and filing petitions, motions, oppositions, replies, discovery requests, and related submissions in inter partes review (IPR), post-grant review (PGR), and covered business method (CBM) patent review proceedings before the USPTO/Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page limits for petitions, motions, oppositions, and replies
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules establish page limits for petitions, motions, oppositions, and replies to improve efficiency and focus issues. The Board’s contested-case experience and federal court practices inform these limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current contested-case standing-order practice: 50-page limit for motions/oppositions on priority, 15-page limit for miscellaneous motions/oppositions (§ 41.121(a)(3), § 41.122), 25-page limit for other motions/oppositions (§ 41.121(a)(2)); replies: 15 pages for priority, 5 pages for miscellaneous, and 10 pages for other motions. Under the final rules: up to 60 pages for an inter partes review petition; 80 pages for a post-grant review petition and for a covered business method petition (post-grant and CBM); a 15-page limit is provided for replies to petitions requesting a trial; oppositions get an equal number of pages as the corresponding motion. Parties may seek a waiver of the page limits by motion showing the waiver is in the interests-of-justice (a copy of the desired non-page-limited petition must accompany the motion). The Board generally decides such waiver motions prior to deciding institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds eligible for review (scope of petitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory limits determine which grounds may be raised in petitions for each type of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter partes review petitions: based upon any grounds identified in 35 U.S.C. 311(b) — i.e., only grounds that could be raised under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 and only on the basis of patents or printed publications. Post-grant review petitions: based upon any grounds identified in 35 U.S.C. 321(b) — e.g., failure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112 (except best mode). Covered business method review is similar in scope to post-grant review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee payment timing and fee-setting factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director must set fees to be paid by the person requesting review; the fee must accompany the petition on filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. 311(a)/321(a) the Director may establish multiple fees based on the aggregate costs of performing the reviews and the complexity of the review. The Office adopted the number of claims for which review is requested as an administrable factor affecting fee amount. Alternatives considered and rejected include: (i) charging by number of grounds (difficult/contentious to determine), (ii) charging by pages of argument (difficult to administer/distinguish argument vs evidence), (iii) charging fees at multiple steps in the process (would hamper timely completion and conflict with 35 U.S.C. 312/322), and (iv) setting reduced fees for small/micro entities or refunds if a review is not instituted (statutory limitations under 35 U.S.C. 41(d)(2)(a), 42(h)(1), 42(d) limit reductions/refunds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee must accompany petition; refunds and small-entity reductions limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees set by the Director must accompany the petition at filing; the Director is not required to provide refunds and fee reductions are constrained by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 312(a)(1) and 322(a)(1) require that the fee established by the Director accompany the petition on filing. The Office concluded it does not have authority to provide refunds when a review is not instituted and that fees set under its authority are not reduced for small entities in the same manner as other fees (cites 35 U.S.C. 41(d)(2)(a), 42(h)(1), and 42(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default electronic filing with limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: All papers are to be electronically filed unless otherwise authorized; exceptions may be granted based on entity size/sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper filing system increases delay and risk; a rigid mandatory electronic-only rule could impose unnecessary burdens where a party lacks ability. The adopted option requires electronic filing by default but allows authorization of alternative filing methods considering entity size and sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery: default limited discovery and standards for additional discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules set a default limited scope of discovery as a matter of right and allow additional discovery only upon meeting specified standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To promote effective discovery, the Board will set a default scheduling order providing limited discovery as a matter of right and permit requests for additional discovery on a case-by-case basis. Inter partes reviews use an 'interests-of-justice' standard for additional discovery (slightly higher than 'good cause'); post-grant and CBM reviews employ a 'good cause' standard. Under interests-of-justice the moving party must show full diligence in seeking discovery and no undue prejudice to the non-moving party; the Board will weigh economic impact on the opposing party (limiting discovery where the opposing party is a small entity). Parties may also agree to additional discovery among themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro hac vice appearance rule and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-registered practitioners may be recognized pro hac vice upon a showing of good cause, subject to conditions and possible revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may recognize counsel pro hac vice during a proceeding upon a showing of good cause and may impose conditions including an acknowledgement that counsel is bound by the Office’s Code of Professional Responsibility. Granting or revoking pro hac vice status is discretionary and may consider factors such as qualifications compared with registered practitioners, genuine need, incompetence, prior misconduct before the Office, unwillingness to abide by the Code, and incivility. Past practice required demonstrating (1) how qualified the unregistered practitioner is relative to a registered practitioner, and (2) whether the party has a genuine need for that particular unregistered practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for instituting a review (statutory constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold for instituting administrative review is set by statute and cannot be lowered below statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office considered but did not adopt a threshold as low as ex parte reexamination because of statutory requirements in 35 U.S.C. 314 (inter partes review) and 324 (post-grant review). The rules implement institution thresholds consistent with those statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for institution decision and reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will decide whether to institute a trial within a set time window tied to filings or waivers; unsuccessful petitions have a route for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will determine whether to institute a trial within three months after the earlier of: (1) submission of a patent owner preliminary response, (2) waiver of filing such a response, or (3) expiration of the time period for filing such a response. If the Office decides not to institute a trial, the petitioner may file a request for reconsideration. The Office estimated that preparing and filing a request for reconsideration will require about 80 hours of professional time (cost estimate provided in the notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-institution motions practice (types, averages, and process references)
rubrics_metrics.description: After institution, parties may be authorized to file motions (e.g., motions to amend, motions for additional discovery), oppositions, and replies; the rules reference many procedural sections for filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice references procedures in many CFR sections for motions, oppositions, and replies (e.g., §§ 42.6, 42.8, 42.11, 42.13, 42.21, 42.22, 42.24, 42.51, 42.52, 42.53, 42.54, 42.63–42.65, etc.). The Office estimates an average inter partes review will have 6 motions/oppositions/replies after institution and an average post-grant or CBM review will have 8. The Office envisions most motions will be decided in a conference call or shortly thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement-related procedures and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may file requests to treat a settlement as business confidential, requests for adverse judgment, or requests to make a settlement agreement available; procedures and fees apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures to treat a settlement as business confidential are set forth in § 42.74(c); requests for adverse judgment in § 42.73(b); requests to make a settlement agreement available in § 42.74(c)(2). The notice estimates professional time and costs: requests to treat a settlement as business confidential — 2 hours ($742); requests for adverse judgment — 1 hour ($371); requests to make a settlement agreement available — 1 hour ($371) plus a fee of $400 specified in § 42.15(d). The notice also estimates drafting a settlement agreement will require ~100 hours ($37,100) if the parties are not also in litigation and ~1 hour ($371) if the parties are in litigation; the Office estimates percentages of reviews with concurrent litigation for burden accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default equality of pages for oppositions and reply page-limits rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositions receive the same number of pages as the corresponding motion; replies have specified page limits; the page-limit framework is justified by efficiency and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.24(b) provides that oppositions are allotted an equal number of pages as their corresponding motions, consistent with federal court practice. Section 42.24(c) provides page limits for replies (e.g., 15 pages for replies to petitions requesting a trial). The Office’s contested-case experience found page limits beneficial in focusing issues, reducing costs, and improving decision times, and informed the chosen numeric limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of authority to the Board for counsel conduct and disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules delegate limited authority to the Board and to the Chief Administrative Patent Judge to regulate counsel conduct and disqualification during proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule delegates to the Board the authority to conduct counsel disqualification proceedings while the Board has jurisdiction over a proceeding, and delegates to the Chief Administrative Patent Judge the authority to make final decisions to disqualify counsel in a proceeding before the Board for purposes of judicial review. This delegation does not derogate the Director’s prerogative nor prevent further delegation to administrative patent judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated practitioner time and cost burdens for common filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice provides estimated professional time and associated cost figures for numerous routine filings to quantify economic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the notice: preparing and filing a patent owner preliminary response — 91.6 hours ($34,000); first patent owner reply/third-party comment in inter partes reexamination combined cost ~$29,000; request for reconsideration — 80 hours ($29,680); oral hearing per party — $6,800 (~18.3 hours at $371/hr); requests to treat settlements as business confidential — 2 hours ($742); adverse judgment request — 1 hour ($371); settlement agreement drafting — 100 hours ($37,100) if not concurrently litigated; submission of a copy of a notice of appeal — ~6 minutes ($37.10). The notice uses these estimates in the regulatory economic analysis and to set and justify fees and procedural limits.
